prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators and for the experimental realisation of the quantum spin Hall state in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep a single-part prize for B039. The scientific case has not weakened. Kane and Mele introduced the Z2 invariant and the time-reversal-protected quantum spin Hall state, and Molenkamp's group saw the quantised edge conductance in HgTe quantum wells. The result has been reproduced and extended by many groups in 2D and 3D materials, and the concept now organises how people search for materials and design devices, including in cold-atom and circuit platforms. That is the kind of new organising principle I look for. It is mature after roughly fifteen to twenty years, and no member argued it is premature. On the chair's question about novelty versus metrology, I weigh a new class of matter above a smaller error bar, but I do not claim that the lattice clock is a lesser science. The chair's questions on the 2016 prize are answered by the scope of that prize: Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz covered topological phase transitions and Chern-type phases, not time-reversal-invariant Z2 physics. I narrow my citation to the 2D quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, with the HgTe realisation, so that Molenkamp is credited for what his experiment showed and not for the prediction.
statement.case_against: The attribution is still the weak point and round 1 did not remove it. The Molenkamp experiment tested the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal and not the original Kane-Mele graphene proposal, Zhang has died, and Fu, Moore, Balents, Roy, Hasan and Cava made the 3D case. If the committee treats the 2D and 3D discoveries as one achievement, no three-person set is fully fair. If it treats them as two, B039 is a compound discovery that does not fit a single prize. I think the 2D citation with the HgTe realisation is defensible, but only with an external priority review of Bernevig, Hughes and Hasan before the final ballot. I am working outside my core field, and four of eight members place B022 first with a much cleaner credit, so I do not claim B039 is beyond reasonable dispute.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B039 with broad wording on prediction and experimental discovery of the quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators, and wants the citation confined to the 2D case, while admitting that the BHZ and 3D omissions are real.
responses.response: I agree on confining the citation to 2D, and I now think it is necessary and not only prudent. The broader phrase on topological insulators would invite the 3D question, where Fu, Moore, Balents, Hasan and Cava would have strong claims that the trio cannot cover. I would keep the wording as Z2 topological insulators in the sense of the Kane-Mele invariant and tie the experimental part explicitly to HgTe quantum wells. I disagree slightly with the word discovery for Molenkamp, since the proposal that made HgTe the right host came from BHZ. Realisation is more accurate and is easier to defend to external reviewers.

responses.point: Mehlig says B022 would win if precision were weighted above novelty, argues the committee should not cut a trio only for tidiness, and sees no overlap between the 2016 prize and time-reversal-protected Z2 physics.
responses.response: Your framing of the decision is the most useful one in the exchange, and I answer it in the same terms. I weigh a new organising principle somewhat above metrological impact, but only when the credit can be defended. That is the real tension, because your point about not choosing on tidiness cuts against my own worry. If the external reviews say the prize is only fair with Bernevig and Hughes, I would not simply cut the trio to hide the problem, and I would then move to B022. On the 2016 prize I agree there is no overlap, because the Z2 invariant, Kramers-protected edge states and the HgTe measurement are not in the Thouless-Haldane-Kosterlitz citation.

responses.point: Pearce moved to B022 as first choice after the openings, valuing the clean two-name credit, the independent confirmation at RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, PTB, NIST and SYRTE near 10^-18, and the distinctness of the magic-wavelength lattice from the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: I take the independent-confirmation argument seriously, and in my own area of precision control of quantum systems I recognise how hard 10^-18 is. You have answered the chair's question about what the lattice clock has delivered beyond an error bar better than I expected: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift and many-body clock physics are real physics. My remaining hesitation is the overlap with Hall and Hansch in 2005 and Wineland in 2012, since Wineland already honoured the control of single quantum systems and ion clocks. I would accept B022 as a fully defensible outcome, and I would be at ease with it if a citation names the magic-wavelength lattice explicitly. I do not agree that the SI redefinition is a reason to wait, and I now think it is a consequence and not a condition.

responses.point: Olsson argues that B022 is an invention that is also a discovery in the statutory sense, that the original idea and early demonstration are localised to Katori, and that the answer to the precedent objection is that the lattice is a distinct invention with its own original experiment.
responses.response: That is a fair answer to the precedent objection, and it changes my view of how serious the overlap is. The magic-wavelength trap is a distinct idea from the comb and from single-ion control, so I no longer regard B022 as a refinement of a rewarded line. I still differ on how to read the statute. An invention that opens new tests of nature is fine, but I would want the committee to be clear that the discovery is what is rewarded, which is why I put the new state of matter first. On the chair's question about two names, I think Ye's accuracy record and Katori's concept are both essential, because without the accuracy demonstration the concept would not have changed what can be measured.

responses.point: Lindroth raises that the credit for B022 omits Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley and the ion-clock groups, and that a clock prize is a measurement tool whose status as a discovery about nature cuts against her own taste for the unexpected.
responses.response: Your candour on that point carries weight with me, because it is the same worry I raised in round 1 about a refinement of existing physics. I also agree that the 10^-18 results are robust. On your credit question, the omission of Lemonde and Ludlow is a less severe problem than the BHZ omission in B039, because the lattice concept is localised to Katori and the accuracy record to Ye. That is the one respect in which your candidate has the cleaner case, and I accept it. I would still ask the Secretary to commission the B022 priority review as a precaution, since neither of us has verified the chronology.

uncertainties: Whether external reviews of the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal and the 3D work will show that Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is a defensible trio for the 2D quantum spin Hall effect, or whether it is unfair without Bernevig and Hughes.
Whether the 2D quantum spin Hall effect and the 3D topological insulators are one achievement or two. I treat the 2D case as the achievement, but that is a judgement and not a verified fact.
Whether the committee should weigh conceptual novelty above metrological impact. I do, but not by much, and a convincing priority review for B022 could change my preferred part.
Whether two superconducting-circuit prizes in consecutive years would be acceptable. I lean no, and I am conflicted on B023 in any case.
Whether a two-part prize is feasible within three people. B039 and B022 name five people, so a subset of one would be needed, and I do not see a fair way to cut it.
statement.conflict_note: I direct WACQT at Chalmers, co-authored the dynamical Casimir effect experiment, and know the circuit-QED community, including Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson as Chalmers colleagues. This is a specific connection to B023, and I would recuse myself from any discussion or vote on it if it advances, which is why it stays only an alternative. Chalmers has hosted 2025 laureates Clarke and Martinis. I have no specific connection to B039, B022, B005 or B025, and no connection to the people credited on the preferred part beyond working in the same broad community of quantum condensed matter.
